section: 1. AI Tooling Disclosure & Five Substantive Reasons to Verify These Numbers Independently
text:
1. AI Tooling Disclosure & Five Substantive Reasons to Verify These Numbers Independently
This reference site and companion PDF brief were initiated and reviewed by Matthew R.V. Ross using Google DeepMind’s Antigravity coding agent to execute an open-source, reproducible R (4.5.2) + Quarto (1.10) pipeline (src/00_setup_theme.R through src/05_verify_audit.R). When evaluating an AI-assisted fiscal analysis on a contested campus topic, readers appropriately ask: “Why should anyone trust these numbers?” Five concrete analytical safeguards—and two places where cross-checking overturned initial assumptions—anchor the answers:

Zero Unverified LLM Memory (Deterministic R Computation From 70 Archived Filings): Not a single dollar amount, headcount, or percentage in any chart or table originates from language-model recall. Script 01_fetch_sources.R downloaded and SHA-256 hashed 70 primary public PDFs, governance memos, and federal/BLS API tables across CSU Office of Budgets, CSU IRP&E Fact Books, CDHE Format 30/20 Budget Data Books, CSU System Audited Financial Statements (FY15–FY25), Colorado Office of the State Auditor (OSA) statutory NCAA Agreed-Upon Procedures reports (2516F-B, 2505F-B), BLS CPI-U (CUUR0000SA0), and Urban Institute IPEDS (2015–2023), logging exact source URLs and page/table references in data/sources_manifest.csv.
Multi-Ledger Accounting Triangulation Across Independent Entities: Every headline claim is cross-checked across at least two independent reporting systems—reconciling CSU internal ColOBS division budgets (B2 Athletics $16.91M FY25 / $17.15M FY26) against Colorado State Auditor NCAA filings (2516F-B), Fact Book FY27 workforce tables against continuous CDHE Format 30 Budget Data Books (FINAL_BDB), and CSU System Financial Statements against U.S. Department of Education IPEDS series.
Testing and Overturning Initial Premises When Primary Data Disagreed:

What overturned the initial “faculty + admin grew equally” premise: Fact Book FY27 (Table 128) makes E&G Faculty appear to jump +43.3% (901.0 → 1,291.0 FTE, FY15–FY25) because pre-2019 "Special" and "Temporary" instructors vanish from active rank tables and reappear in FY19–FY20 as newly formalised "Contract" and "Continuing" (CCA) faculty under the April 2018 Faculty Manual Section E reform. Triangulating against continuous CDHE Format 30 Budget Data Books shows true continuous E&G Faculty FTE grew +7.2% over nine years (1,528.6 in FY17 → 1,638.5 in FY26, -0.8% vs. FY20) and Tenured/TT grew +2.2%, whereas E&G Administrative Professional FTE rose +62.3% (FY15–FY25), including +30.6% (+326.3 FTE) after FY22 (62.1% in Central VP/Admin/Spur units).
Where headline-only critiques fall short mathematically: Simultaneously, testing headline flashpoints against CSU’s $885.16M FY26 E&G budget and $66.0M FY28 midpoint gap shows B2 Athletics ($17.15M) + XA Debt Service ($31.86M) equal 5.5% of E&G (8.0% of 10-year E&G growth), and cutting 100% of net Athletics support (~$15.57M) plus $1.43M in recent transition payouts still leaves ~76% (~$50M/yr) of the FY28 shortfall unresolved.

Disaggregating Self-Supporting Grants & Controlling Accounting Transfers: Rather than treating all-funds staff ratios (~3:1) as uniform E&G overhead, Fact Book Table 123–124 isolates 69.7% (3,205.5 of 4,597.7) of FY25 Administrative Professional FTE funded outside E&G (Sponsored Programs, Other Funds, Recharge Centers, Auxiliaries across units such as CIRA, CEMML, VTH, AES, Extension, and CSFS). Likewise, ColOBS division analyses adjust explicitly for FY19’s $41.64M aid shift (XA to P1) and FY26’s ~$111.26M pooled fringe decentralization so accounting transfers are never mislabeled as organic spending spikes.
Independent Two-Way Verification & Open Programmatic Assertions (src/05_verify_audit.R): Claims circulating from both administration and faculty critics were independently verified against public filings and press archives—confirming the $1.10M Parsons and $325k Underwood settlements ($1.43M combined), Coach Mora’s $2.4M–$2.8M base / $1.5M UConn buyout package, and zero CSU employment tie for Title IX consultant Jeff Lamoureux. Seven programmatic checks in src/05_verify_audit.R verify all ledger balances and partitions on every build, and all source scripts and processed tables are published openly so any reader can inspect or challenge every calculation.

Corrections, missing primary citations, or alternative accounting interpretations from any member of the CSU community are welcomed via github.com/matthewross07/csu_budget_context.

2. Accounting Scope & Deflation Notes

CSU System vs. Fort Collins Standalone Scope (finstmt2015–2025 vs. BDB/ColOBS/OSA):

CSU System Audited Statements combine Fort Collins, CSU Pueblo, and System/SPUR ($644.9M net tuition, 21.3% discount rate, $1,330.7M long-term debt in FY25 + $79.1M STRATA ATLAS Laser bonds issued June 26, 2025).
Fort Collins Standalone Scope comes from CDHE Format 30/20 Budget Data Books (FINAL_BDB), CSU Office of Budgets Operating Budget Summaries (ColOBS + OBS), IRP&E Fact Books (Tables 122–128), and Note 5 of Colorado OSA Report 2516F-B ($1,118.77M Fort Collins total debt, including $206.96M Athletics debt).

Real-Dollar Deflation (CPI-U, macro_cpiu_fy.csv):

Monthly BLS CPI-U All Urban Consumers (CUUR0000SA0, 2014–Oct 2026) is averaged across CSU’s July–June fiscal calendar so multi-year net tuition and debt series are evaluated in constant FY25 or FY26 purchasing power (FY27 covers Jul–Oct 2026).

title: Athletics Accounting & Long-Term Capital Debt Context
text: Placing a $75.24M gross Athletics budget alongside a $61.3M–$70.7M E&G operating gap makes it natural to ask whether restructuring or reducing Athletics could close the university’s shortfall. Audited filings from the Colorado Office of the State Auditor (csu_ncaa_aup_fy19.pdf–fy25.pdf, Report 2516F-B) clarify both perspectives: Athletics receives meaningful ongoing institutional support (~15–20% of Ledger B’s multi-year structural pressures), yet gross expenditure numbers substantially overstate how much general-fund cash could be freed quickly.

1. Enrollment Shifts & Higher-Margin Non-Resident Mix (~$25.00M)

title: Understanding CSU’s FY27–28 Operating Budget Gap
text:
Topline Takeaway: Structural debt, executive transition payouts ($1.10M presidential + $325k provost = $1.43M one-time), and Athletics institutional support (~$15.57M/yr net operating, $206.96M bonded debt) are material parts of Colorado State University’s fiscal picture. Yet on CSU’s $885.16M FY26 Education & General (E&G) budget, Athletics E&G base support (B2: $17.15M, 1.9%) and central debt service (XA: $31.86M, 3.6%) represent 5.5% of the operating budget and 8.0% of 10-year E&G growth (FY15–FY26). Even cutting 100% of net Athletics support and executive transition payouts would leave roughly ~$49M–$50M/yr (~76%) of the projected $66.0M FY28 shortfall unresolved, pointing toward broader structural drivers: non-resident enrollment mix, expiring one-time stopgaps, flat state support under TABOR, rising tuition discounting, and permanent E&G payroll growth—especially post-FY22 E&G Administrative Professional hiring (+30.6%), while continuous CDHE E&G Faculty FTE grew +7.2% (FY17–FY26).
Ahead of the Nov. 30 AAUP chapter meeting, Dec. 1 Faculty Council, and Dec. 3–4 Board of Governors meetings, this reference separates near-term FY28 operating mechanics (Ledger A) from multi-year structural context (Ledger B) using 70 archived primary public documents logged in data/sources_manifest.csv. High-level budget files cannot capture the operational value of specific campus services or teaching units; rather, these figures provide a common factual baseline across faculty, staff, deans, central administration, and the Board.

Long-term growth in E&G Admin Pro (+62.3% FY15–FY25; +30.6% post-FY22), legacy incremental budgeting, doubled System debt ($1.33B), and a 21.3% tuition discount rate.


Executive Payouts ($1.43M Combined)
One-time $1.10M presidential + $0.325M provost settlements equal 2.2% of one year's midpoint gap ($0 recurring).
Material governance & transparency issue rather than a core recurring financial driver.


Athletics ($75.2M Gross Budget)
Minimal year-over-year change unless net university transfers expand.
Meaningful ~17% structural pressure (~$15.6M net operating support) + $206.96M bonded debt.


Externally & Self-Funded Staff
Do not drive the E&G shortfall; funded by grants, contracts, clinical fees & auxiliaries.
Account for 69.7% of all AP FTE; separating them keeps general-fund comparisons accurate.

Why Trust an AI-Assisted Analysis? Verification Checks Built Into This Pipeline

Methodological Verification (AI + R/Quarto Transparency): This site and companion PDF brief were constructed using Google DeepMind’s Antigravity coding agent driving a deterministic R (4.5.2) + Quarto (1.10) pipeline (src/00–src/05). Because automated tools and rapid campus narratives can both introduce errors, five substantive verification checks anchor every figure:

Zero Unverified LLM Memory: Not a single dollar figure, headcount, or percentage comes from LLM memory or back-of-the-envelope prompting. Every number is computed programmatically from 70 downloaded primary public filings and federal/BLS API extracts logged with exact URLs and SHA-256 digests in data/sources_manifest.csv.
Multi-Ledger Accounting Triangulation: Major claims are cross-checked across independent state, system, and federal records—reconciling CSU ColOBS B2 allocations ($16.9M–$17.2M) against Colorado State Auditor NCAA reports (2516F-B), Fact Book FTE tables against continuous CDHE Format 30 Budget Data Books, and CSU System Audits against IPEDS (2015–2023).
Testing and Overturning Initial Assumptions When Data Disagreed: An early premise behind this analysis assumed both faculty and administrative hiring overshot enrollment equally (+43% vs. +62% in Fact Book FY27). Cross-checking Fact Book rank tables against CDHE Format 30 and CSU’s April 2018 Faculty Manual Section E overhaul overturned that premise: Fact Book FY27 omits retired "Special" and "Temporary" codes from historical tables, making 2018–19 rank formalization look like net faculty hiring. On a continuous CDHE Format 30 basis (FY17–FY26), E&G Faculty grew +7.2% (and Tenured/TT +2.2% over FY15–FY25), whereas E&G Admin Pro surged +62.3% (FY15–FY25), including +30.6% (+326.3 FTE) after FY22—supporting faculty concerns on administrative expansion while still establishing mathematically that headline cuts ($1.43M payouts + ~$15.6M net Athletics) leave ~76% of Ledger A unsolved.
Separating Self-Supporting Research Staff & Controlling Accounting Shifts: General-fund (E&G) roles are strictly isolated from externally and self-funded research, clinical, extension, and auxiliary staff (69.7% of all AP FTE in Table 123–124), and historical ColOBS budgets control explicitly for FY19’s $41.64M financial-aid shift (XA to P1) and FY26’s ~$111.26M fringe decentralization.
Open Code, Reconciled Sums & Two-Way Fact-Checking (src/05_verify_audit.R): Automated verification assertions test all ledger balances and fund partitions on every build, and independent checks verify personnel and contract claims across multiple viewpoints (confirming $1.43M combined executive settlements and Coach Mora’s $2.4M Pac-12 package while finding no CSU employment record tying Title IX consultant Jeff Lamoureux to Fort Collins). Full documentation appears on How This Was Built.

Empirical Finding That Overturned an Initial Assumption: Reading CSU Fact Book FY27 (Table 128 / rank tables) in isolation makes total E&G faculty appear to jump +43.3% (901.0 → 1,291.0 FTE between FY15 and FY25) because E&G Continuing and Contract ranks jumped from 2.2 FTE in FY15 to 332.2 in FY20. Cross-checking CSU’s April 2018 Faculty Manual Section E reform and continuous CDHE Format 30 Budget Data Books (FINAL_BDB_FY17-18–FY26-27) reveals that jump was largely an administrative reclassification, not net new faculty hiring:

In April 2018, Faculty Council replaced legacy "Special" and "Temporary" non-tenure-track labels with structured Contract, Continuing, and Adjunct (CCA) tracks; departments migrated existing instructors across FY19–FY20. text:
2. State Funding Limits, Tuition Discounting & Research F&A Mechanics




Accounting-Adjusted E&G Division Trends (FY15–FY26), Institutional Discounting Rate, and Non-Resident Mix



Three structural revenue constraints help explain why active teaching schedules and record external grant volume do not automatically close an E&G operating gap:

Rising Institutional Tuition Discounting: In CSU System audited financial statements (audits_system_fy15_fy25), scholarship allowances increased from $114.4M (19.9% discount rate in FY15; 17.9% in FY17) to $174.1M (21.3% discount rate) in FY25. Within Fort Collins E&G budgets (bdb_real_fy17_fy27), institutional aid grew from $47.2M (FY15) to $88.5M (FY26) and $96.3M estimated for FY27, offsetting part of nominal tuition rate increases (3.5% resident / 4.0% NR / 3.5% differential in FY27).
State Funding Constraints: In FY27 (obs_state_approp_fy24_fy27), State Fee-for-Service ($161.60M) and COF stipends ($49.45M) supply $211.05M (23.4% of the $900.98M State Appropriated / E&G budget)—virtually flat versus FY26 ($210.94M) under Colorado’s TABOR limits and state Medicaid pressures.
Why Sponsored Research Grants Do Not Directly Cross-Subsidize E&G Instruction: CSU System grants and contracts reached $548.0M in FY25 (audits) and Fort Collins Indirect Cost Recovery (IDCR) reached $76.0M (obs). Federal F&A recovery only partially reimburses dedicated research compliance, startup packages, cost-share commitments, and laboratory infrastructure rather than generating discretionary cash for general undergraduate instruction.

1. Leadership Transition Payouts, Football Contracts & Personnel Record Checks

Verified Executive Settlements & Athletics Commitments

Combined FY26–FY27 Executive Transition Payouts ($1.43M One-Time Total):

Presidential Settlement ($1.10M): On Oct. 28, 2026, CSU announced President Amy Parsons’ resignation effective Dec. 31, 2026 (prior contract ran through Jan. 2028; Rick Miranda assumes Interim Presidency Jan. 1, 2027), alongside a $1.10M transition payout (due by Jan. 5, 2027, covering the remaining contract period plus roughly five additional months of salary) and a mutual non-disparagement agreement—prompting criticism from AAUP-CSU on Nov. 5 (aaupcsu.org) and student reporting in The Rocky Mountain Collegian.
Provost Settlement ($325,000): Former Provost & EVP Marion Underwood departed the role in early 2026 with a $325,000 settlement agreement documented in CSU public reporting before later becoming provost at George Mason University.
Fiscal Scale Context: Combined, the $1.425M in recent senior leadership settlements raises legitimate governance and confidentiality concerns, yet as a non-recurring expense it represents 2.2% of one year’s $66.0M FY28 operating gap and $0 in ongoing base savings.

Football Coaching Transition Package ($2.4M Starting Base): Head football coach Jim Mora Jr. was hired Dec. 1, 2025 on a 5-year contract escalating from $2.4M (2026) to $2.8M (2030), alongside a $150k signing bonus, a $1.5M UConn buyout paid by CSU, and an expanded assistant salary pool reported around $5M ahead of CSU’s Pac-12 transition. Reducing head coaching base pay alone resolves less than 4% of Ledger A, whereas overall Athletics net institutional support (~$15.57M/yr) and bonded debt ($206.96M) are examined in Athletics & Debt.



Independent Record Check: Title IX Consultant Jeff Lamoureux

Source Verification Note: Several campus emails and organizing discussions cited the hiring of Title IX investigator Jeff Lamoureux (also spelled Lamoureaux) alongside San Francisco Chronicle reporting as evidence of executive vetting lapses at CSU. Independent verification across CSU directories and public news archives does not confirm a CSU employment tie:

Public records: External Title IX consultant Jeff Lamoureux (CIXE) previously held Title IX coordination roles at universities outside Colorado (including Appalachian State University). Meanwhile, CSU’s official Office of Title IX Programs and Gender Equity leadership and staff roster—alongside The Rocky Mountain Collegian archives—does not list Jeff Lamoureux (note that a separate CSU student disability spokesperson, Anicee Lamoreaux, shares a similar surname). Separately, San Francisco Chronicle photojournalism involving CSU and Title IX in 2024–2025 covered Mountain West volleyball litigation rather than an investigator hire.
Why precision helps: Anchoring campus oversight discussions in documented local records—such as the $1.43M combined transition settlements, mutual non-disparagement clauses, B2/OSA Athletics support ($17.15M / ~$15.57M net + $206.96M debt), and post-FY22 E&G Admin Pro hiring (+30.6%)—keeps shared governance centered on undisputed facts.

Three comparative patterns emerge from IPEDS FY23:

Colorado State Funding Per FTE Trails Out-of-State Land-Grants: At $7,314 in state appropriations and grants per student FTE, CSU receives roughly half the per-student state support of Washington State ($17,679/FTE), Utah State ($16,171/FTE), and Kansas State ($15,112/FTE)—while still receiving more than 3× CU Boulder ($2,326/FTE). All three Colorado campuses rely substantially on tuition revenue (27.6% of current revenue at CSU; 39.5% at CU Boulder; 40.0% at Mines).
CSU Carried Relatively High Long-Term Debt Per FTE ($38,915/FTE): Among comprehensive R1 land-grants in this group, CSU’s $38,915/FTE ($1,118.6M FY23 IPEDS debt) exceeds Oregon State ($31,252/FTE), Kansas State ($23,638/FTE), Washington State ($21,804/FTE), CU Boulder ($20,634/FTE), Utah State ($16,632/FTE), and Iowa State ($15,507/FTE), trailing only specialized Colorado School of Mines ($106,552/FTE).
CSU’s All-Funds Staff Ratio (3.29x) Sits Mid-Pack: CU Boulder (3.93x), Kansas State (3.90x), Iowa State (3.43x), and Washington State (3.41x) all report higher non-instructional-to-instructional IPEDS headcount ratios than CSU (3.29x), confirming why examining general-fund (E&G) staffing patterns since FY22—rather than all-funds totals containing externally funded research, clinical, and extension personnel—provides the clearer institutional benchmark.

text:
3. Constructive Questions Ahead of the FY28 Hybrid RCM Transition
In their Oct. 26, 2026 memo (alongside Faculty Fellows Rob Mitchell and Jennifer Martin), university leadership stated directly that changing the budget model will not by itself close a budget shortfall or generate new revenue. With FY27 serving as the Parallel Year ahead of July 1, 2027 implementation, campus discussions can focus productively on four areas:

Disaggregate Post-FY22 E&G Central VP Hiring (864.8 FTE = 62.1% of E&G AP): Share clearer breakdowns showing how much of the +326 E&G Admin Pro increase between FY22 and FY25 reflects student retention, mental-health, compliance, IT security, or classified-to-AP conversions versus central administrative expansion—keeping externally funded research, clinical, and extension staff clearly separate.
Co-Design Transparent FY28 Hybrid RCM Rules: Publish clear parameters ahead of Dec. 3–4 BOG review covering “off-the-top” central assessments (XA Debt Service $31.86M, CSU Spur $15.00M), credit-hour allocation weights, and instructional subvention rules for foundational disciplines.
Align Long-Term Athletics & Debt Planning With E&G Capacity: Evaluate multi-year glide paths for CSU’s ~$15.6M net Athletics operating support (B2 $17.15M FY26 base) alongside prudent policies on any new bonded or internal treasury debt while general funds remain tight.
Track Net Tuition Yield Alongside Enrollment Headcounts: As campus recruits both resident and non-resident cohorts (-9.7% Dom NR UG in Fall 2026), evaluate net revenue per seat after institutional discounting ($174.1M System allowance / 21.3% discount rate) alongside gross headcount goals.
